newsitem.title: USA: India official calls Enron project a "success".
newsitem.headline: India official calls Enron project a "success".

text.p: Despite legal problems that plagued Enron Corp's effort to build a power plant in India, the project was a success because it will pave the way for similar projects to go more smoothly, Indian officials told U.S. investors on Tuesday.

Indian officials and business leaders, eager to attract foreign investment to infrastructure projects, spoke about Enron's $2.3 billion power plant at an India Infrastructure Conference sponsored by Robert Fleming Inc. on Tuesday,

Enron travelled a checkered path of high-profile contract litigation in its effort to build the power plant in India's western Maharashtra state after India opened the sector to foreign investors as part of the economic reforms begun in 1991.
T.S.R. Subramanian, Cabinet Secretary of India, said Enron was caught between warring political factions whose "posturing" developed into headline-grabbing drama.
"It was an act of fate," he lamented.

But Subramanian noted that the government set a precedent by winning all 24 cases brought to court against the Enron contract. After Enron, none of the other seven power projects encountered political problems, so in retrospect the project was a success, he said.
"The judgement will go a long way," he said. "The court will not entertain frivolous cases" in the future.
Anil Ambani, a managing director of Reliance Industries, said the Enron saga demonstrated the "resilience the Indian system has displayed."
The disputes were resolvled through arbitrations, and power generation will start on schedule in 1998, he said.

Shankar Acharya, Chief Economic Advisor to India's Finance Ministry, told U.S. investors that despite recent political turmoil following the change of prime minister, there was a consensus among all the 14 parties of the coalition that economic reform must continue.
As a result, the pro-growth budget that passed in May continued enjoying strong support, he said.
